clues: Under heavy traffic the site suddenly starts failing to load, then recovers on its own a few minutes later.
The failures line up with spikes in concurrent users, not with a code deploy or config change.
Error logs mention the app can't get a database connection, yet the database itself shows low CPU and is responsive.
The number of open connections to the database caps out at a fixed small number no matter how much traffic grows.
The connection pool max size is too low and connections aren't returned fast enough, so every pooled connection is checked out and new requests block until they time out.
A page that lists items gets slower and slower as the list grows, even though each item is simple.
Response time scales with the number of rows returned, not with the complexity of any single row.
The server log shows one query to fetch the list, then a separate near-identical query for almost every single row.
The repeated queries all fetch the same related child table keyed by the parent id.
The ORM lazy-loads the child relation inside a loop, issuing one query per parent row instead of a single joined or batched query (the classic N+1).
A search that used to feel instant now takes many seconds, and only started slowing down recently.
The slowdown began around the time the table passed a few million rows.
The slow query filters or sorts on a column that is used in almost every request.
EXPLAIN shows the database doing a full sequential scan of the whole table for that query.
The frequently filtered or sorted column has no index, so the planner scans every row; adding a B-tree index removes the seq scan.
Two people editing the same record sometimes lose each other's changes without either of them noticing.
The lost data only shows up when two saves happen within the same second or two.
The save path reads the current value, computes a new value in the app, then writes it back.
Neither write checks whether the record changed since it was read; both overwrite the whole row.
There is a read-modify-write without locking or optimistic concurrency (no version check), so concurrent transactions clobber each other's updates (a lost update).
Every so often the database gets a brief, intense burst of identical heavy queries, then goes quiet.
The spikes happen like clockwork at regular intervals rather than with traffic.
The burst always follows the moment a popular cached item's time-to-live runs out.
Many requests all see the cache miss at the same instant and each triggers the same expensive lookup.
At TTL expiry all clients recompute the value simultaneously (a cache stampede); fix with single-flight/locking or early refresh with jittered TTLs.
Some scheduled jobs ran an hour early or late on a particular day, and only that day.
The off-by-an-hour events all happened around the start or end of daylight saving time.
Timestamps are stored and compared as local wall-clock times instead of absolute instants.
Two events an hour apart collapsed into the same timestamp, or an hour went missing or repeated.
The code treats naive local times as absolute, so the DST spring-forward/fall-back shift moves scheduled times; store UTC and convert only for display.
A service that ran fine for days starts getting sluggish, then crashes with out-of-memory.
Restarting the process fixes it temporarily, but memory climbs steadily again afterward.
Memory usage grows with the number of requests handled, not with the size of any single request.
A profile shows objects (caches, listeners, or closures) are allocated and never released.
References are held longer than needed (e.g. an ever-growing cache or uncleared event listeners), so the garbage collector never reclaims them; a memory leak.
Rarely, two unrelated actions both fail at the same time with no obvious cause.
The failures happen only when the two operations run concurrently and in opposite orders.
Each failing transaction holds a lock the other one needs to proceed.
Logs show both transactions were rolled back by the database as victims of a cycle.
Two transactions acquire the same rows in different orders, forming a lock cycle the DB resolves by killing one (a deadlock); serialize lock order or keep transactions short.
After logging in, users randomly get logged out or see empty carts as they click around.
The problem only appears once traffic is spread across more than one server.
Each request sometimes lands on a different backend instance than the previous one.
Session state lives in memory on the instance that first handled the login, not in a shared store.
Requests aren't pinned to the instance that holds the session (no sticky sessions and no shared session store), so a different instance can't see the session.
Names with accents or emoji show up as question marks or weird symbols after saving.
The corruption only happens for non-ASCII characters; plain ASCII is fine.
The bytes are correct in the browser but wrong once they reach the database or a file.
Some layer is decoding UTF-8 bytes as Latin-1 (or a similar mismatch) somewhere in the pipeline.
Text is interpreted with the wrong character encoding (e.g. UTF-8 read as Latin-1), so multibyte characters get mangled; set UTF-8 end to end.
A known-good integration suddenly starts getting rejected even though its calls are valid.
The rejections began after that client's normal traffic grew a bit busier than usual.
The errors are 429 Too Many Requests keyed by the client's IP or account.
The limit is a fixed threshold with no allowance for this client's expected volume.
A one-size-fits-all rate limit treats a legitimate high-volume client as abuse; use an allowlist or per-tier quotas.
The last page of results is either empty or shows one item repeated from the previous page.
Users report the final record is missing, or that scrolling never quite ends.
The bug appears exactly at the boundary between two pages of data.
The slice uses something like limit/offset with an inclusive end instead of exclusive.
The pagination uses an off-by-one (e.g. offset..offset+limit inclusive, or wrong < versus <=), dropping or duplicating the boundary row.
After updating a record, the old value keeps showing up for a while.
A refresh or just waiting fixes it, and the stale view isn't consistent across users.
The read path serves a cached value that was never cleared when the data changed.
Writes update the database but never touch the corresponding cache key.
The cache key isn't invalidated (or updated) on write, so reads serve the previous value until it expires; a stale cache.
Right after a deploy or restart, the service is slow to become healthy and sometimes falls over.
The trouble is a single huge spike the moment the service comes back online.
Every connected client reconnects and re-requests everything at the exact same instant.
There's no staggering: all background jobs and warm-up tasks fire simultaneously on boot.
On restart all clients and workers wake at once (a thundering herd); add jitter, backoff, and lazy warm-up so load ramps instead of spiking.
Totals are off by a cent here and there, and never by a round amount.
The discrepancies show up only for certain prices or quantities, not others.
The math looks correct in code but the stored or displayed numbers have long decimal tails.
Values are stored and added as binary floating point (float/double).
Money is computed with binary floats, so rounding error accumulates (e.g. 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3); use integer cents or decimal types.
